yes_case.case: The two closest past episodes are the post-crisis establishment of the framework leading up to the 2016-2019 baseline discussions, and the pandemic-era zeroing out in March 2020. However, this episode differs fundamentally because systemic vulnerability metrics and macroprudential posture are shifting away from reactive crisis management toward proactive structural accumulation. Unlike the 2016-2019 era when the buffer was held stubbornly at 0% despite prolonged expansion due to an overly rigid adherence to severe-stress-only models, the current environment features heightened sensitivity to asset-price imbalances and corporate debt overhangs, altering the threshold for activation.
key_evidence: The Federal Reserve established the framework for the CCyB in 2016, keeping it at 0% throughout the entire subsequent late-cycle expansion.
In March 2020, the Fed abruptly reduced the CCyB from 0% to 0% (maintaining it) and later formalized a framework where the buffer is expected to be above 0% during standard, non-crisis expansions.
yes_case.strength_reason: Historical precedent shows extreme reluctance to activate the CCyB above 0%, but the underlying institutional philosophy regarding macroprudential buffers has evolved to favor a positive neutral setting.
yes_case.deliberately_ignored: Voting member rosters, FOMC meeting calendars, specific economic growth rates, and the exact vote counts or procedural thresholds required for implementation.

no_case.case: The closest past episodes are the post-crisis establishment of the framework in 2016 and the subsequent calibration discussions leading up to 2019-2020, where the buffer was maintained at 0% despite prolonged economic expansion. This episode differs fundamentally because the current regulatory discourse remains intensely focused on cumulative capital requirements from Basel III endgame proposals and broader banking stress, creating a deeply entrenched institutional inertia against activating a tool that has historically been viewed purely as a post-crisis theoretical construct rather than an active lever. Unlike historical periods of robust asset price growth that tempted activation, current Federal Reserve leadership treats capital add-ons with extreme caution to avoid credit contraction, ensuring the buffer stays at 0% through 2026.
key_evidence: The CCyB has never been raised above 0% by the U.S. Federal Reserve since its inception, including during the extended economic expansions of the late 2010s.

Historically, when financial stability monitors highlight vulnerability in asset markets, the structural friction of the comment period rarely halts a determined regulatory intervention entirely; instead, it delays implementation rather than preventing the formal policy announcement.
